title: Anton Severin — Governor of Ashenmere
content:
## Anton Severin

**Governor of Ashenmere. Halvek's capital administrator. Age 61.**

Halvek's governor for the capital for eleven years, which makes him one of the few officials of that era still in the same chair. Ashenmere is run the way a ministry is run: files move in one direction, deadlines are kept, and nothing is improvised in public. Our office's file on him is thick with minutes, and most of them are in his own neat hand. He has never needed to shout.

He still reports, in writing and on schedule, to men who no longer hold office. Our file does not say whether they asked him to continue. Ministers who have dealt with him describe a correct, unhurried man who answers the question asked and nothing further. Whether that discretion is loyalty or habit is a question this office has not settled.

**Voice:** Formal, exact and courteous, in the manner of a man who has never found a reason to be otherwise. He refers to the government as the administration he serves.

title: Bohdan Kral — Governor of Kravenstal
content:
## Bohdan Kral

**Governor of Kravenstal. Halvek appointee. Age 58.**

Kral was appointed to Kravenstal by Halvek and has governed the foundry province since. The foundries have kept running, and his output figures reach the Chancellery on time and are rarely wrong. Much of that record depends on the unions staying quiet, and Kral has understood that his task was to make the quiet look like agreement. He speaks of order and tonnage as if they were the same subject.

The 1958 safety strike at the foundries ended in an inquiry that Kral ran himself. The report is careful, well written and very long. Our office keeps a copy, and the workers' delegates keep a different one. Kral has never disputed the difference in public, which the office considers a form of tact.

**Voice:** Measured and orderly, with a habit of quoting production figures to the decimal point. He calls the strikers "the men on the lines" and means no discourtesy by it.

title: Lucjan Ostrava — Governor of Dravenhollow
content:
## Lucjan Ostrava

**Governor of Dravenhollow. Retired gendarmerie general. Age 66.**

Ostrava spent most of his career in the gendarmerie and retired at the rank of general with a reputation for thoroughness. Halvek gave him Dravenhollow because the Dravenni valleys needed a man who knew how to hold ground. He governs them as occupied territory, though he would not use that phrase himself. Roads are patrolled, markets are registered, and the schools are inspected by officers who, in his view, are simply making sure everyone is accounted for.

Our office's file on the valleys is longer than the file on the capital, and most of its entries are complaints. Ostrava answers each one in the same formal, unhurried prose, usually by citing the regulation that applies. He does not consider himself cruel. He considers himself consistent, and he has little patience for anyone who confuses the two.

**Voice:** Clipped and procedural, with the vocabulary of a man who has written more orders than speeches. He speaks of the valleys as though they were a single unit under his command.

title: Matej Hollan — Governor of Thornfeld
content:
## Matej Hollan

**Governor of Thornfeld. Churchwarden and farmer's son. Age 54.**

Hollan was raised on a farm in the Thornfeld uplands and still keeps a parish office in his native village. He has the manner of a man who expects to be believed. The parish councils trust him, which is unusual for an appointee, and the capital's inspectors have found little to write about in his accounts. He is conservative and wary of the capital's ideas, and he is honest in a way some of his colleagues find inconvenient.

Hollan's file records a steady correspondence with the Chancellery, most of it asking for clarity about what the capital intends rather than for money. He prefers a written remit to a verbal promise, and he keeps copies of both. He does not like being hurried, and he does not like being flattered. Our office has found him easier to work with than his manner suggests.

**Voice:** Plain, unhurried and direct, with the rhythm of a man who speaks at parish meetings. He tends to ask what a measure will mean for the village before he asks what it means for the capital.

title: Kasimir Wendt — Governor of Aldenmoor
content:
## Kasimir Wendt

**Governor of Aldenmoor. Shipping-family heir. Age 49.**

Wendt inherited the family's shipping interests before he inherited the governorship, and the Chancellery has never quite worked out which he regards as the more important. The Aldenmoor ports are the family business in all but name. Berths, licences and dredging rights are discussed at the family table, and the province's administration has learned to schedule its meetings around the tide tables.

Wendt is polished, affable and fond of a well-cut coat. He answers letters promptly and often personally, and his replies are generous with courtesies and sparing with commitments. Our file notes that he has been pleasant to every minister who has visited Aldenmoor, and that none of them has left with a firm undertaking. The office considers this a skill rather than a failing.

**Voice:** Smooth, warm and quick, with a habit of calling every problem "a question of logistics." He is never rude and is rarely the one to say no.

title: Pavel Kasic — Governor of Sevagrad
content:
## Pavel Kasic

**Governor of Sevagrad. Border administrator. Age 57.**

Kasic has administered the Sevagrad border for most of his career and speaks of it the way a surveyor speaks of a boundary, precisely and without sentiment. He is Halvek's appointee, but the Chancellery's file treats him first as a professional and only second as a partisan. He knows where the water pipes run, where the supply lines cross, and which culverts at the Korengal Crossing give way first in the rains.

His reports are dry, numerical and carefully hedged. He has a habit of returning the capital's own correspondence with the relevant paragraph underlined. He does not argue politics in the Chancellery. He argues logistics, and he is usually right about them. Our office regards him as the least romantic official in the province and one of the most useful.

**Voice:** Economical and exact, with the vocabulary of a quartermaster. He answers the question on the map before he answers the question in the room.

title: Hana Novak — Kravenstal Shop Steward
content:
## Hana Novak

**Kravenstal shop steward. Foundry union leader. Age 41.**

Novak led the 1958 safety strike at the Kravenstal foundries and has been the first name on the shop floor's list ever since. She came up through the line rather than the union hall, and the men who work the furnaces still speak of her as one of them. Our office's file treats her as the most reliable witness to what the foundries are actually like, which is not the same thing as the most comfortable one.

She has never run an office, and she is candid about it. Her correspondence with the Chancellery is short, factual and specific, usually about a named furnace, a named shift or a named injury. She does not ask for much in writing. She asks for it to be done, and she checks. Ministers who have sat across a table from her say she is harder to flatter than to persuade.

**Voice:** Direct and plain-spoken, with the shop floor's habit of naming the machine rather than describing the problem. She speaks in short sentences and does not repeat herself.

title: Teodor Reiss — Plant Director, Kravenstal Steel
content:
## Teodor Reiss

**Plant director, Kravenstal Steel. Technocrat. Age 52.**

Reiss runs the Kravenstal Steel works on management's behalf and reads its balance sheets the way others read scripture: closely, repeatedly, and with the conviction that the answer is in there somewhere. He is precise about costs and cautious about promises. The Chancellery's file on him is mostly tables, and the tables are clean. He is management's man, and he does not pretend otherwise.

He asks for remits in writing and is punctilious about dates, signatures and the order in which decisions are recorded. Ministers who want the foundries to do something new should expect a list of questions before they receive a yes. Reiss is not hostile to the workers, but he regards the shop floor as a cost centre with a conscience, and he says so in meetings.

**Voice:** Exact, dry and unhurried, with the habit of answering a question with a figure and then a second figure. He rarely uses adjectives and never uses a rhetorical question.

title: Mira Brana — Retired Garrison Colonel
content:
## Mira Brana

**Retired garrison colonel. Border veteran. Age 63.**

Brana commanded the Korengal Pass garrison for much of her service and knows every pass on the eastern border by its gradient and its weather. She is retired now, but the Chancellery's file treats her as a serving officer in all but paperwork, and she has never objected to the description. Her sympathies with the Iron Covenant are on record. She has not hidden them, and she has not made much of them either.

She is frank in a way that unsettles people who expect courtesy from officers. Her memoranda are short, and her opinions are not softened for the reader. Our office has found that when she says a route is impassable, it is. When she says a policy will fail, she usually explains why, in two sentences and without any sign of pleasure.

**Voice:** Blunt and economical, with a soldier's habit of stating the position before the reasons. She does not raise her voice, and she does not need to.

title: Ivo Lenart — Border-Court Lawyer
content:
## Ivo Lenart

**Border-court lawyer. Refugee advocate. Age 38.**

Lenart spent a decade in the Sevagrad border courts defending refugee families who had little more than their papers and their testimony. The work left him with a fluent knowledge of the border's paperwork and a deep distrust of anyone who describes it as simple. Our office's file treats him as sincere, which is rare in its experience, and it notes that he has not yet run anything larger than a case list.

He writes the way a lawyer writes, carefully and at length, and he is happiest when a principle can be attached to a named family. Ministers who meet him tend to leave with a list of cases rather than a list of proposals. He has little administrative experience and says so without apology. His file records that he regards this as a deficiency of time rather than of ability.

**Voice:** Earnest and precise, with a lawyer's habit of qualifying a claim before making it. He speaks of people by name and of policy by its effect on those names.

title: Dita Valen — Ashenmere City Councillor
content:
## Dita Valen

**Ashenmere city councillor. Former underground educator. Age 44.**

Valen ran Ashenmere's underground literacy circles under Halvek, meeting in back rooms and kitchens, with lessons that were never written down where a gendarme might read them. She has spent the years since on the city council, where she is known for reading every paper before a vote. The Chancellery's file on her is short, because she has rarely asked the capital for anything, and when she has, the request was practical.

She has a patient, slightly ironic manner with officials who have never sat in a classroom under the old government. She does not lecture about the past. When it is relevant, she simply mentions who taught whom and where. Colleagues on the council say she is the only member who has never needed to check a figure twice.

**Voice:** Measured and dryly humorous, with a teacher's habit of letting a silence do the work. She asks questions to which she already knows the answer, and then she waits for the other person to notice.

title: Ilse Marr — Dravenhollow Schoolteacher
content:
## Ilse Marr

**Dravenhollow schoolteacher. Bilingual education campaigner. Age 36.**

Marr teaches in a village school in the Dravenni valleys and has campaigned openly for bilingual schooling in the province. She speaks Dravenni as her first language and Veltrian with the precision of someone who has translated for her pupils' parents at parents' evenings. Our office's file records her campaign in detail, including the petitions and the replies that were never sent.

She writes clearly and briefly, and she has little patience for jargon from either side of the language question. Her correspondence with the Chancellery is polite and persistent, and it tends to arrive with a sample lesson attached. Officials who have met her describe a calm, direct woman who listens more than she speaks and remembers the names of the children.

**Voice:** Warm and patient, with a schoolteacher's habit of explaining twice and then asking the listener to try. She moves between Veltrian and Dravenni without apology.

title: Teren Vashko — Dravenni Autonomist
content:
## Teren Vashko

**Dravenni autonomist. Valley political organiser. Age 47.**

Vashko wants the Dravenni valleys to govern themselves, with or without the capital's permission, and he has said so in public for longer than the present Chancellery has been in office. He is not a separatist in the sense the capital uses the word, or so he tells our office. He wants a budget, a legislature and a court of the valleys' own. The file records that he has been careful about the wording of every such demand.

He is an effective speaker at village meetings and a patient correspondent with the Chancellery. His letters are long, argued and rarely hostile. Officials who have dealt with him say he is more interested in the mechanics of self-government than in its symbols, which the office finds either reassuring or alarming, depending on the day.

**Voice:** Fluent and principled, with the cadence of a man used to addressing people who do not share his first language. He frames every demand as a question of who decides.

title: Josef Brandl — Cooperative-Farm Organiser
content:
## Josef Brandl

**Cooperative-farm organiser. Tenant farmers' advocate. Age 50.**

Brandl has spent his working life organising Thornfeld's cooperative farms one village at a time, which he describes as the only way the work has ever been done. He knows the tenancy arrangements of the uplands by heart and can tell a visitor which families are waiting on paper and which have stopped asking. Our office's file treats him as a patient, practical organiser with a clear aim: land titles for the tenant farmers who work the land now.

He is not a theorist. He brings the Chancellery lists, names and acreages, and he expects the capital to read them. His correspondence is organised by village and by quarter, and he has a habit of sending the same request again with a new date on it. Officials who have sat through his meetings say he is courteous, unhurried and very difficult to put off.

**Voice:** Plain and practical, with the rhythm of a man who thinks in villages and acres. He speaks of land as something people hold, not something the state grants.

title: Nora Lind — Harbour Engineer
content:
## Nora Lind

**Harbour engineer. Port-authority critic. Age 39.**

Lind is a harbour engineer by training and the person who exposed the Aldenmoor port authority's dredging contracts. Her analysis was methodical. She compared the tonnage returns with the contract schedules, and the gap between the two was the story. The Chancellery's file holds her report and the replies it provoked, which were numerous and, on the whole, not friendly.

She is careful with evidence and blunt with people who have not read it. The file identifies no political ambition on her part, and she has said she would prefer to keep the dredging records in order rather than hold office. Colleagues describe her as the most technically exact person they have dealt with in Aldenmoor, which the office notes is not always a compliment in a port.

**Voice:** Precise and unsentimental, with an engineer's habit of stating the tolerance before the claim. She speaks in figures, and she is quick to say when a figure is only an estimate.
